questions.stem: A deep vein in one leg becomes obstructed, increasing pressure in vessels upstream. What local change most directly favours swelling?
options: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure
A decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure
An increase in plasma albumin concentration
An increase in lymphatic drainage capacity
questions.explanation: Impaired venous drainage raises capillary pressure and promotes movement of fluid from capillaries into interstitial tissue. Why not the alternatives: Higher plasma oncotic pressure or stronger lymphatic removal would oppose fluid accumulation.

questions.stem: After firm stroking of the skin, redness spreads beyond the directly stimulated line. What produces this surrounding flare?
options: Closure of all precapillary sphincters around the area
Direct filtration of red blood cells into the epidermis
Clotting of capillaries at the site of injury
An axon reflex causing nearby arterioles to dilate
questions.explanation: The flare of the triple response is produced by an antidromic axon reflex that dilates vessels around the stimulated region. Why not the alternatives: The wheal reflects increased local permeability, whereas the flare is spreading arteriolar vasodilation.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, cuff pressure is slowly released during blood-pressure measurement. Disappearance of Korotkoff sounds usually marks which pressure?
options: Mean arterial pressure
Pulse pressure
Systolic pressure in the brachial artery
Diastolic arterial pressure
questions.explanation: As cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the brachial artery is open throughout the cardiac cycle and the characteristic Korotkoff sounds generally disappear. Why not the alternatives: The first appearance of sound usually marks systolic rather than diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: A patient develops rapidly rising intracranial pressure with impaired brainstem perfusion. Which combination is typical of the Cushing response?
options: Increased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Decreased arterial pressure with complete loss of sympathetic tone
Increased arterial pressure with sustained reflex tachycardia
Decreased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
questions.explanation: Reduced medullary perfusion causes a powerful sympathetic rise in systemic pressure. The resulting arterial hypertension stimulates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia. Why not the alternatives: The raised pressure is a compensatory response to brainstem ischemia; bradycardia is secondary to the baroreflex.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the key physical restriction to paracellular movement across the blood–brain barrier?
options: Endothelial tight junctions.
The choroid plexus epithelium.
Loose junctions of cerebral venules.
Astrocytic end-feet alone.
questions.explanation: Tight junctions in cerebral capillary endothelium restrict movement between cells; astrocytes support barrier function. Not B: The choroid plexus forms a separate blood–CSF barrier. Not C: Loose venular junctions would not account for selective restriction. Not D: Astrocytes help maintain the barrier but are not the main sealed endothelial layer.

questions.stem: Why does the sinoatrial (SA) node normally determine the heart rate?
options: Its impulses reach ventricular myocardium faster than those in Purkinje fibres.
It reaches the threshold for spontaneous discharge sooner than other pacemakers.
Its cells have a more negative resting membrane potential than ventricular cells.
It produces the largest action potential of all pacemaker cells.
questions.explanation: The SA node has the highest normal intrinsic pacemaker rate. Its impulses reach subsidiary pacemakers before those slower sites discharge. Why not the alternatives: Blood supply, contraction strength and ventricular conduction speed do not set the normal pacemaker hierarchy. Other conducting tissues also show automaticity.

questions.stem: Two beats have different QRS heights. A student concludes the taller complex produced a larger stroke volume. What is the main flaw?
options: QRS height measures the amount of venous blood returning.
QRS height represents the duration of ventricular contraction.
QRS height directly records the pressure within the ventricle.
QRS height reflects voltage, not the amount of blood ejected.
questions.explanation: The ECG measures electrical potentials. A larger recorded deflection may reflect electrical orientation or amplitude; it does not directly quantify mechanical stroke volume. Not A: Venous return is a haemodynamic variable not directly measured by the tracing. Not B: Duration is measured horizontally on ECG paper, not from complex height. Not C: A surface ECG records electrical potential rather than ventricular pressure.
questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Why does most left ventricular coronary blood flow occur during diastole rather than systole?
options: Pulmonary venous pressure becomes higher than aortic pressure during systole.
Contracting left ventricular muscle compresses vessels within its wall.
The left coronary artery is closed by the aortic valve during systole.
The heart stops using oxygen during systole.
questions.explanation: During left ventricular systole, high intramyocardial pressure compresses coronary vessels, especially in the subendocardium. Relaxation during diastole permits better perfusion. Why not the alternatives: Coronary arterial openings remain connected to the aorta; the critical factor is compression by contracting myocardium.

questions.stem: Two ventricular function curves are compared at the same end-diastolic volume. Curve X produces a greater stroke volume than curve Y. What best explains the difference?
options: Ventricular preload must be greater on curve X.
The ventricular muscle must be less responsive to calcium on curve X.
Ventricular contractility is greater on curve X.
The heart rate must be lower on curve X.
questions.explanation: An upward shift of the Frank-Starling curve indicates greater stroke volume at the same preload, consistent with increased contractility. Why not the alternatives: The comparison holds end-diastolic volume constant, so increased preload is not the explanation; reduced calcium response would tend to reduce contractility.

questions.stem: Inflation of the lungs sends sensory impulses towards the medulla. What cardiovascular response is described in the lecture?
options: Vagal afferent inhibition of vasomotor activity with vasodilation.
Carotid sinus chemoreceptor inhibition with increased arterial tone.
Atrial volume-receptor excitation with sustained vasoconstriction.
Sympathetic afferent excitation of vasomotor activity with constriction.
questions.explanation: The lecture states that lung-inflation afferents travel in the vagus and can inhibit the vasomotor centre, lowering vascular tone and pressure. Not B: The carotid sinus is a stretch receptor, and the described effect is dilation. Not C: This is a lung-inflation input rather than an atrial filling response. Not D: The named afferent pathway is vagal and its effect is depressor.

questions.stem: What change occurs in the pulmonary circulation with the newborn's first breaths?
options: The ductus venosus begins carrying blood from the right ventricle.
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises as alveolar oxygen rises.
Systemic vascular resistance falls because the placenta remains connected.
Pulmonary vascular resistance falls as the lungs expand and oxygen rises.
questions.explanation: Lung expansion and increased alveolar oxygen reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, raising pulmonary blood flow. Loss of the placenta simultaneously tends to raise systemic vascular resistance. Why not the alternatives: The first breaths promote pulmonary vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric contraction, which pressure relationship initiates opening of the aortic valve?
options: Left ventricular pressure first exceeds aortic pressure.
Aortic pressure rises above left ventricular pressure.
Left atrial pressure rises above left ventricular pressure.
Pulmonary arterial pressure falls below left atrial pressure.
questions.explanation: The aortic valve opens once left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, ending isovolumetric contraction and beginning ventricular ejection. The valve opens because the pressure gradient reverses, not simply because the ventricle contracts. Why not the alternatives: When aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, the aortic valve remains closed. Left atrial and pulmonary arterial pressures do not determine its opening.

questions.stem: After bleeding stops, both haemoglobin and plasma-protein concentrations fall as circulating volume recovers. What explains this?
options: New red-cell production lowers haemoglobin concentration.
Venoconstriction selectively removes haemoglobin from blood.
Added fluid dilutes the remaining blood components.
Raised renal filtration removes most circulating proteins.
questions.explanation: Fluid recruited from tissues or given intravenously restores volume before red-cell and protein mass recover, producing dilution. Not A: New red-cell production raises rather than lowers haemoglobin mass. Not B: Venoconstriction redistributes blood rather than removing haemoglobin. Not D: Renal filtration is generally depressed during acute severe shock.

questions.stem: The cerebral aqueduct becomes blocked while CSF production continues. Which ventricles are expected to enlarge first?
options: The fourth ventricle alone
The third and fourth ventricles only
The lateral and third ventricles
The fourth ventricle and central canal only
questions.explanation: The aqueduct links the third to the fourth ventricle. Obstruction causes CSF to accumulate upstream in the third and lateral ventricles. Why not the alternatives: The fourth ventricle lies downstream of the aqueduct and is not the primary site of enlargement in an isolated aqueduct blockage.
questions.subtopic: CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and lumbar puncture

questions.stem: What prevents ventricular myocytes from sustaining a normal tetanus?
options: Systolic calcium release becomes too small to sustain successive twitches.
Spontaneous pacemaker activity prevents ventricular re-excitation.
Ventricular muscle has a refractory period shorter than its twitch.
Refractoriness lasts through most of contraction.
questions.explanation: The long action potential and absolute refractory period prevent rapid re-excitation and mechanical summation into tetanus. Not A: Cardiac cells repeatedly generate action potentials. Not B: Calcium channels are essential for the cardiac plateau. Not C: Cardiac muscle contains actin and myosin.

questions.stem: In a lead where the QRS is upright, the T wave is often upright too. Which combined explanation best accounts for this?
options: Repolarisation has the same polarity but travels in the reverse direction.
Repolarisation has opposite polarity and generally travels in the reverse direction.
Repolarisation has the same electrical sign and travels in the same direction through the ventricles.
Repolarisation has opposite polarity but travels in the same direction.
questions.explanation: A repolarisation wave has the opposite electrical sign to depolarisation; ventricular repolarisation also progresses in the reverse order, producing a T wave often concordant with QRS. Not A: Reversed direction without the polarity reversal would also favour opposite deflections. Not C: Depolarisation and repolarisation do not have the same electrical polarity. Not D: Opposite polarity without reversed direction would favour opposite QRS/T deflections.
questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Mean arterial pressure is 95 mmHg and intracranial pressure is 15 mmHg. Assuming cerebral venous pressure is not higher than intracranial pressure, what is cerebral perfusion pressure?
options: 65 mmHg
95 mmHg
75 mmHg
80 mmHg
questions.explanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is approximately MAP - ICP when ICP is the effective downstream pressure: 95 - 15 = 80 mmHg. Why not the alternatives: Perfusion pressure is a difference between driving and downstream pressures; it is not the MAP alone.

questions.stem: Left ventricular pressure has risen to 45 mmHg. Left atrial pressure is 10 mmHg and aortic pressure is 85 mmHg. Which phase is most likely?
options: Isovolumetric contraction
Isovolumetric relaxation
Reduced ventricular ejection
Rapid ventricular filling
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. The aortic valve remains closed because ventricular pressure is still below aortic pressure. Rising pressure with both valves closed indicates isovolumetric contraction. Why not the alternatives: Ejection requires ventricular pressure above aortic pressure, while filling requires ventricular pressure below left atrial pressure.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a forearm artery is briefly blocked and then restored. Why may flow temporarily rise above its resting level?
options: Venous outflow rises suddenly and forces extra blood through the artery.
Restoration of pressure directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle.
The release of occlusion briefly raises systemic arterial pressure.
Accumulated metabolites continue to dilate local vessels.
questions.explanation: During the occlusion, tissue oxygen delivery falls and local vasodilatory signals build up. When flow resumes, dilated resistance vessels produce transient reactive hyperaemia. Why not the alternatives: Reactive hyperaemia is a temporary local response to preceding flow interruption.

questions.stem: Why can prolonged renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation worsen heart-failure oedema?
options: It causes sustained urinary sodium loss.
It decreases circulating volume and filling pressure.
Salt and water retention raises venous pressure.
It prevents compensatory arterial vasoconstriction.
questions.explanation: RAAS initially supports blood pressure, but prolonged salt and water retention increases filling pressures and oedema. Not A: Aldosterone promotes sodium retention rather than loss. Not B: RAAS tends to expand, not deplete, extracellular volume. Not D: Angiotensin II supports rather than blocks vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: According to Poiseuille's law, if a vessel radius is reduced to half while other factors remain constant, how does resistance change?
options: It becomes 4 times greater.
It becomes 16 times greater.
It becomes roughly two times greater.
It becomes 8 times greater.
questions.explanation: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Halving radius therefore increases resistance by 2^4 = 16 times. Why not the alternatives: The fourth-power dependence is stronger than a linear, square or cubic change.

questions.stem: Damage selectively removes the inhibitory effect of the medullary depressor area on the pressor area. Which response is expected?
options: Reduced sympathetic discharge with markedly decreased vascular tone.
Greater vagal discharge with isolated venous dilation.
Greater sympathetic discharge with increased vascular tone.
Reduced local metabolism with fixed arteriolar diameter.
questions.explanation: The depressor area normally inhibits the pressor area; removing this brake permits more sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity. Not A: Disinhibition would increase, not decrease, pressor drive. Not B: A selective loss of pressor inhibition does not primarily increase vagal output. Not D: Local tissue metabolism is not directly abolished by this lesion.

questions.stem: A person loses a substantial amount of blood. What sequence most directly explains the initial fall in cardiac output?
options: Lower blood volume directly raises ventricular end-diastolic volume.
Lower blood volume raises pulmonary venous return above systemic venous return.
Lower blood volume immediately increases plasma oncotic pressure enough to raise output.
Lower blood volume leads to lower venous return and ventricular filling.
questions.explanation: Blood loss reduces circulating volume and venous return, which reduces preload and stroke volume. Reflex vasoconstriction may defend pressure but cannot automatically restore lost flow. Why not the alternatives: Loss of circulating volume does not directly raise preload or stroke volume.

questions.stem: A drug markedly inhibits SERCA in cardiac muscle. What change in relaxation is expected?
options: Slower calcium removal impairs relaxation.
Its calcium influx through L-type channels immediately increases.
Shorter calcium transient and stronger relaxation.
Faster removal of calcium from cytosol.
questions.explanation: SERCA normally resequesters calcium into the SR; inhibiting it prolongs the cytosolic calcium transient and slows relaxation. Not B: SERCA inhibition does not directly abolish membrane L-type channels. Not C: Less reuptake prolongs rather than shortens the cytosolic transient. Not D: Calcium removal becomes slower, not faster.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, a PR interval extends across 4.5 small squares. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: 0.24 s, above the stated PR-interval range.
0.90 s, above the stated PR-interval range.
0.09 s, shorter than the stated normal PR-interval range.
0.18 s, inside the stated PR-interval range.
questions.explanation: The horizontal duration is 4.5 × 0.04 = 0.18 s. This lies within the 0.12–0.20 s interval given in the lecture. Not A: This is not the product of 4.5 and 0.04 s. Not B: This incorrectly assigns 0.20 s to each small square. Not C: This incorrectly halves the duration obtained from 4.5 small squares.

questions.stem: A patient develops headache that is worse upright after lumbar CSF sampling. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: The procedure obstructs both foramina of Monro.
Persistent CSF leakage lowers intracranial CSF pressure.
Lumbar puncture increases CSF production several-fold.
The sample immediately increases blood–brain barrier permeability.
questions.explanation: Leakage from the dural puncture can reduce CSF pressure and cause a characteristic postural headache. Not A: The foramina are far from the lumbar puncture site. Not C: Production does not normally surge to cause this symptom. Not D: BBB disruption is not the usual cause of post-lumbar-puncture headache.
questions.subtopic: CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and lumbar puncture

questions.stem: Why does inspiration normally widen the split between the aortic and pulmonary components of the second heart sound?
options: More right-heart filling delays pulmonary valve closure.
Reduced right ventricular filling delays aortic valve closure.
Increased right ventricular filling delays mitral valve opening.
Increased left ventricular filling delays tricuspid valve closure.
questions.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, often prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying P2 relative to A2. Why not the alternatives: S2 reflects semilunar valve closure, not AV valve opening or closure.

questions.stem: A patient with left ventricular failure develops breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. What pressure change most directly promotes fluid movement into the lungs?
options: Increased lymphatic drainage with unchanged capillary pressure
Increased pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased plasma oncotic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Decreased hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
questions.explanation: Poor left ventricular output raises pressure upstream in the left atrium and pulmonary veins. Higher pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes filtration and pulmonary oedema. Why not the alternatives: Fluid filtration increases with raised hydrostatic pressure; higher oncotic pressure would tend to oppose it.

questions.stem: Rapid infusion of fluid increases venous return and stretches the right atrium. Which reflex response may help accommodate the larger venous return?
options: Heart rate may remain unchanged because atrial stretch has no reflex effects.
Heart rate may increase as atrial stretch activates a reflex.
Heart rate rises because the fluid infusion has reduced carotid sinus pressure.
Heart rate may decrease because atrial stretch directly increases vagal outflow.
questions.explanation: The atrial stretch (Bainbridge) reflex can increase heart rate when venous return and atrial filling rise. It is distinct from the arterial baroreceptor response to elevated blood pressure. Why not the alternatives: Atrial distension can elicit reflex tachycardia without requiring arterial hypotension. The infusion increases rather than reduces venous return.

questions.stem: Aortic pressure suddenly rises. For the first affected beat, ventricular filling and contractility are unchanged. What is the likely effect on stroke volume?
options: Stroke volume increases because ventricular filling has increased.
Stroke volume increases because aortic recoil becomes stronger.
Stroke volume stays constant because heart rate has not changed.
Stroke volume decreases with greater aortic afterload.
questions.explanation: Greater afterload makes ventricular ejection more difficult. Before compensatory adjustments, end-systolic volume tends to increase and stroke volume decreases. Why not the alternatives: Aortic recoil, filling and AV conduction are not the mechanisms determining the first-beat afterload response.

questions.stem: Why can a cerebral arterial branch occlusion cause a local infarct despite the Circle of Willis?
options: Small distal territories may have limited effective collateral flow.
The basilar artery can supply every distal cortical branch directly.
Every cerebral artery has a complete set of parallel branches.
Cerebral veins normally replace arterial inflow after blockage.
questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis provides proximal connections, but distal cerebral arterial territories have limited functional anastomoses. Not B: Basilar inflow does not directly replace all distal arterial territories. Not C: Distal vessels are not completely interconnected. Not D: Veins drain blood and cannot substitute for oxygenated arterial supply.

questions.stem: An ECG develops a new shift of the ST segment above or below the baseline. Which process specifically makes this segment clinically important?
options: Normal atrial depolarisation creates the ST deflection of each beat.
The onset of valve closure normally lifts the ST segment above baseline.
A decrease in cardiac preload directly determines ST segment height.
Myocardial ischaemia or inadequate oxygenation can alter ST level.
questions.explanation: Ventricular ischaemia or hypoxia can disturb membrane potentials and cause ST elevation or depression, so the segment is useful in recognising myocardial injury patterns. Not A: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave and normally precedes ST. Not B: ST displacement is an electrical finding, not the normal marker of valve closure. Not C: Preload is a filling variable and does not directly set ST height.
questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Oxygen consumption is 280 mL/min. Arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous oxygen content is 130 mL/L. What is cardiac output?
options: 5 L/min
2 L/min
4 L/min
3 L/min
questions.explanation: Arterial-mixed venous oxygen content difference = 200 - 130 = 70 mL/L. Cardiac output = 280 mL/min divided by 70 mL/L = 4 L/min. Why not the alternatives: The Fick method divides oxygen consumption by the oxygen content difference, not by either concentration alone.

questions.stem: Which observation most strongly points to a myogenic rather than metabolic adjustment?
options: Dilation follows reduced tissue oxygen supply.
Dilation follows accumulation of local lactate.
Constriction follows a rise in vessel-wall stretch.
Constriction follows removal of excess local metabolites.
questions.explanation: The myogenic response is the smooth muscle reacting to stretch itself: more stretch → more contraction. Responses driven by O₂, CO₂, H⁺, lactate or other chemicals are metabolic. Not A: Low oxygen is a metabolic signal for dilation. Not B: Lactate accumulation is a metabolic signal for dilation. Not D: Metabolite washout belongs to metabolic autoregulation.

questions.stem: Why is the normal T wave generally broader than the QRS complex?
options: The T wave corresponds to ventricular contraction rather than electricity.
Ventricular repolarisation usually takes longer than its depolarisation.
The T wave covers atrial and ventricular depolarisation together.
Ventricular depolarisation spreads more slowly than repolarisation.
questions.explanation: The T wave reflects the slower process of ventricular repolarisation, while QRS represents rapid ventricular depolarisation through the conduction system. Not A: The T wave is still an electrical event, not the force of contraction. Not C: Atrial and ventricular depolarisation are represented mainly by P and QRS. Not D: The statement reverses the usual relative time courses.
questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: A resting adult has a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg. Using the usual resting approximation, what is mean arterial pressure?
options: 95 mmHg
75 mmHg
85 mmHg
90 mmHg
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = 120 - 75 = 45 mmHg. MAP is approximately diastolic pressure + one-third of pulse pressure = 75 + 15 = 90 mmHg. Why not the alternatives: MAP is not the simple arithmetic midpoint; diastole usually occupies more time at rest.

questions.stem: Portal hypertension promotes ascites partly by increasing which force?
options: Hydrostatic pressure in hepatic sinusoids.
Interstitial lymphatic pumping efficiency.
Arterial oxygen tension in the hepatic vein.
Plasma oncotic pressure within hepatic capillaries.
questions.explanation: Higher sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure increases fluid filtration and hepatic lymph formation; excess can enter the peritoneal cavity. Not B: Improved lymphatic clearance would tend to oppose accumulation. Not C: Oxygen tension is not the main Starling-force mechanism. Not D: Higher plasma oncotic pressure would oppose outward fluid filtration.

questions.stem: An older patient faints shortly after standing to urinate at night. Which phenomenon does this episode most closely illustrate?
options: Carotid sinus syncope caused by neck pressure.
Septic shock due to widespread inflammatory vasodilatation.
Micturition syncope linked to reflex hypotension.
Positive-g blackout from head-level underperfusion.
questions.explanation: Micturition syncope is fainting associated with urination, often after rising at night, due to a reflex pressure fall. Not A: Carotid sinus syncope requires stimulation of a sensitive carotid region. Not B: There is no evidence of infection-related shock in the stem. Not D: Normal standing to urinate is not high positive acceleration.

questions.stem: Why might severe anaemia produce a cardiac flow murmur despite structurally normal valves?
options: Anaemia markedly increases blood viscosity and suppresses flow.
Lower viscosity and increased flow favour turbulence.
Anaemia blocks the ventricular conduction system.
Reduced blood volume necessarily closes the aortic valve.
questions.explanation: Anaemia lowers viscosity and may increase cardiac output, raising the tendency to turbulent flow and a functional murmur. Not A: Anaemia decreases viscosity rather than increasing it. Not C: Conduction block is not the principal mechanism of flow murmurs. Not D: The murmur is not due to forced aortic valve closure.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, consecutive ECG R waves are separated by 20 small horizontal squares. What is the ventricular rate?
options: 100 beats/min
75 beats/min
60 beats/min
80 beats/min
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, one small square = 0.04 s. Twenty squares = 0.8 s per beat, giving 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min. Equivalently, 1500/20 = 75 beats/min. Why not the alternatives: Heart rate depends on the R-R interval; the standard 25 mm/s conversion yields 1500 divided by small squares.

questions.stem: Immediately after a person stands up quickly, before reflex compensation has fully developed, what tends to happen?
options: Venous pooling decreases and ventricular filling rises.
Cardiac output rises because gravity pushes blood toward the chest.
Venous pooling increases and venous return to the heart falls.
Venous pressure in the feet falls below pressure at heart level.
questions.explanation: Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure and pooling in dependent veins. This reduces central venous return, initially lowering stroke volume and potentially cerebral perfusion. Why not the alternatives: Without compensation, standing does not drive leg blood centrally or raise head-level perfusion.

questions.stem: How can an impulse spread rapidly between adjacent cardiac muscle cells?
options: Gap junctions provide low-resistance electrical connections.
Each cell must first receive a motor-neuron endplate signal.
Mechanical desmosomes independently generate pacemaker signals.
The connective tissue between cells conducts sodium current.
questions.explanation: Gap junctions in intercalated discs permit ion current to spread from cell to cell, supporting a functional syncytium. Not B: Cardiac muscle does not require motor endplates for every contraction. Not C: Desmosomes provide mechanical attachment rather than electrical conductance. Not D: Connective tissue does not replace electrically coupled membranes.

questions.stem: Why does fetal haemoglobin load oxygen effectively at the placental interface?
options: It binds 2,3-BPG more tightly than adult haemoglobin.
Its weaker 2,3-BPG binding increases oxygen affinity.
Its alpha-globin chains bind more oxygen than maternal alpha chains.
Each fetal haemoglobin molecule carries more oxygen binding sites than adult haemoglobin.
questions.explanation: HbF interacts less with 2,3-BPG, shifting its oxygen dissociation curve left and favouring oxygen uptake from maternal blood. Not A: Stronger 2,3-BPG binding would lower oxygen affinity. Not C: Fetal haemoglobin still contains iron-bearing haem groups. Not D: Oxygen binding is reversible, not permanent.

questions.stem: An organ's flow remains nearly constant as its perfusion pressure rises across the autoregulatory range. Which vascular adjustment produces this plateau?
options: Arteriolar resistance falls as perfusion pressure rises.
Venous blood begins flowing backward into the artery.
Cardiac output stops changing throughout the entire body.
Arteriolar resistance rises as perfusion pressure rises.
questions.explanation: For approximately constant flow Q, a higher perfusion pressure requires a higher local resistance (Q = pressure difference / resistance). The plateau reflects autoregulatory adjustment. Why not the alternatives: Falling resistance alongside increasing pressure would increase, rather than stabilize, flow.

questions.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL and an end-systolic volume of 56 mL. What is its ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: Stroke volume = 140 - 56 = 84 mL. Ejection fraction = (84/140) x 100 = 60%. Why not the alternatives: 84 mL is the stroke volume, not a percentage; 40% is the fraction remaining after systole.

questions.stem: During exercise, pulmonary blood flow increases greatly but pulmonary arterial pressure rises relatively little. What helps explain this?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance increases in direct proportion to flow.
The alveoli stop exchanging gases while blood flow rises.
Previously underperfused capillaries open and existing vessels widen.
Most pulmonary capillaries close as flow increases.
questions.explanation: Recruitment of additional pulmonary capillaries and distension of vessels increase the total flow capacity, limiting the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure. Why not the alternatives: Recruitment and distension expand, not reduce, pulmonary vascular capacity.

questions.stem: A patient with severe infection has widespread arteriolar dilation and low arterial pressure. Which shock mechanism is most likely?
options: Distributive shock from widespread loss of vascular tone
Cardiogenic shock caused mainly by poor ventricular pumping
Obstructive shock caused mainly by mechanical blockage of blood flow
Hypovolaemic shock caused mainly by external blood loss
questions.explanation: Sepsis can produce profound vasodilation and loss of vascular tone, lowering total peripheral resistance and effective perfusion pressure. This is distributive shock. Why not the alternatives: The defining event in this stem is widespread low resistance rather than haemorrhage, pump failure or obstruction.

questions.stem: Why is average blood-flow velocity normally much lower in capillaries than in the aorta?
options: Capillaries receive a smaller total blood flow than the aorta in steady state.
The total capillary cross-sectional area is smaller than that of the aorta.
The combined cross-sectional area of all capillaries is much larger.
Lower capillary pressure alone explains the slower movement of red cells.
questions.explanation: For a given volume flow rate, average velocity equals flow divided by cross-sectional area. The enormous total capillary area produces low average velocity. Why not the alternatives: Flow continues in capillaries; the key comparison is total cross-sectional area, not the diameter of one capillary.

questions.stem: A patient has low arterial oxygen and high carbon dioxide. Which peripheral sensors respond mainly to these chemical changes?
options: The atrial type A and type B volume receptors.
The carotid bodies and the aortic bodies.
The carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors.
The sinoatrial and atrioventricular pacemaker nodes.
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, chiefly stimulating breathing. Not A: Atrial volume receptors principally detect filling and stretch. Not C: Arterial baroreceptors principally detect stretch. Not D: Cardiac nodes generate and conduct impulses rather than monitor arterial chemistry.

questions.stem: Which feature most reliably distinguishes first-degree AV block from second-degree AV block in the chapter’s basic ECG classification?
options: Both have identical PR intervals on each beat.
First-degree conducts every P; second-degree drops some.
First-degree lacks P waves; second-degree lacks QRS complexes.
Both show independent P-wave and QRS rhythms.
questions.explanation: First-degree block delays conduction but retains a QRS after every P wave. In second-degree block, at least some atrial impulses fail to produce QRS complexes. Not A: Second-degree block is defined by intermittent failed conduction, not identical PR intervals. Not C: Both conditions can show P waves and QRS complexes on the trace. Not D: Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms indicate complete third-degree block.

questions.stem: At the same stroke volume and heart rate, which change generally increases myocardial oxygen demand more?
options: Pumping against a much higher arterial pressure
Lowering wall tension during ventricular ejection
Pumping against a lower arterial pressure
Reducing the pressure needed to open the aortic valve
questions.explanation: Pressure work, which increases with afterload and myocardial wall tension, carries a high oxygen cost. Pumping the same volume against greater arterial pressure is more demanding. Why not the alternatives: The alternative changes reduce pressure load rather than increase it.

questions.stem: Immediately after arterial pressure falls during haemorrhage, which autonomic response follows reduced arterial baroreceptor firing?
options: Reduced sympathetic and reduced vagal activity together
Increased vagal activity with arteriolar dilation
Increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal activity
Reduced sympathetic activity and increased vagal activity
questions.explanation: Less stretch of carotid and aortic baroreceptors reduces afferent firing. The medulla responds with increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic outflow. Why not the alternatives: Increased vagal activity would tend to slow the heart rather than compensate for falling pressure.

questions.stem: A patient has near-normal resting cardiac output but very high ventricular filling pressures and pulmonary congestion. Which statement fits best?
options: Heart failure can occur with normal output.
High filling pressure proves adequate pumping.
Normal resting output excludes heart failure.
Heart failure requires reduced ejection fraction.
questions.explanation: Heart failure includes states where output is maintained only at abnormally high filling pressures, causing congestion. Not B: High filling pressures can be evidence of dysfunction rather than normality. Not C: A near-normal output can be maintained at harmful filling pressures. Not D: Diastolic failure can occur with preserved ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A patient develops chronic swelling of an arm after axillary lymph nodes are removed. What is the main reason?
options: Plasma albumin production increases sharply in the affected tissue.
The local arterial inflow rises more than the venous outflow can accommodate.
Protein-rich tissue fluid cannot drain through the lymphatics.
Venous pressure is elevated, increasing filtration through intact capillaries.
questions.explanation: Damage to lymphatic pathways reduces the return of interstitial fluid and proteins to the blood, producing lymphoedema. Why not the alternatives: Lymphoedema is caused by impaired lymph removal, not complete loss of arterial flow.

questions.stem: Why is aVF classed as an augmented unipolar limb lead?
options: It compares two fixed chest electrodes in the horizontal plane of the heart.
It uses the left-foot electrode against an averaged limb reference.
It compares the right arm directly against the left arm.
It uses the right-leg electrode as its positive terminal.
questions.explanation: In aVF the left-foot electrode is positive and is compared with an average reference derived from the two arm electrodes. Not A: Chest electrodes make up V1–V6 and mainly examine the horizontal plane. Not C: Right arm versus left arm describes bipolar Lead I. Not D: The right-leg electrode is used for electrical noise reduction.

questions.stem: One group of alveoli is poorly ventilated while nearby alveoli are well ventilated. What happens to the small pulmonary arteries supplying the poorly ventilated region?
options: They dilate through the same low-oxygen response as systemic arterioles.
They dilate, directing more blood toward the poorly ventilated alveoli.
They constrict, directing more blood toward better-ventilated alveoli.
They constrict in response to reduced systemic pressure rather than local oxygen.
questions.explanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary arteriolar constriction. This helps divert flow toward alveoli where oxygen uptake is more effective. Why not the alternatives: The pulmonary hypoxic response is opposite to the usual local hypoxic vasodilation in systemic tissues.

questions.stem: Which isolated change increases the tendency for turbulent flow in a blood vessel?
options: A substantial rise in whole-blood viscosity
An increase in blood-flow velocity
A decrease in blood density
A decrease in vessel diameter
questions.explanation: Reynolds number increases with velocity, density and diameter, and decreases with viscosity. Increased velocity therefore makes turbulence more likely. Why not the alternatives: Higher viscosity and smaller diameter generally lower Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.

questions.stem: Venous return rises while heart rate, afterload and contractility remain unchanged. What immediate change is expected in a normal ventricle?
options: A rise in stroke volume with a fall in end-diastolic volume
A fall in stroke volume despite a rise in end-diastolic volume
A fall in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A rise in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
questions.explanation: More venous return increases ventricular filling and stretches cardiac fibres. On the ascending Frank-Starling relationship this raises force and stroke volume. Why not the alternatives: The Frank-Starling response links greater preload to greater output within physiological limits.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the normal x descent from the y descent in a JVP trace?
options: x: atrial relaxation; y: emptying through the open tricuspid.
x: aortic valve opening; y: mitral valve closure.
x: atrial contraction; y: ventricular isovolumetric contraction.
x: ventricular ejection; y: pulmonary arterial recoil.
questions.explanation: The x descent reflects atrial relaxation and downward tricuspid movement; the y descent follows tricuspid opening as blood empties rapidly. Not B: Left-heart valve events do not define these JVP descents. Not C: Atrial contraction creates the a wave. Not D: Both descents reflect right atrial pressure changes rather than the proposed events.

questions.stem: In complete AV dissociation, an atrium sometimes contracts while the tricuspid valve is closed. Which jugular venous finding may appear?
options: Loss of the y descent with every normal beat
A persistently absent a wave
Intermittent giant a waves
Intermittent giant v waves caused by atrial systole
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve causes a sudden large rise in right atrial pressure, producing cannon or giant a waves. Why not the alternatives: The a wave reflects atrial contraction; the v wave mainly reflects atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed.
